metadata.note: The New York Central's coal railroad. The Toledo & Ohio Central and its subsidiary Kanawha & Michigan ran from the Kanawha Valley mines of West Virginia north through the heart of Ohio's coal counties, through Columbus, to the Toledo lakefront coal docks -- and on this single-track road moved almost a quarter of all the coal on the entire NYC System. Its ancestor, the Atlantic & Lake Erie of 1869, was chartered to link Toledo with Pomeroy on the Ohio River and deliberately bypassed Columbus to the east to reach the coal; that line was finished Toledo-Middleport in 1882 and rebranded the Toledo & Ohio Central in 1885. Buying the Toledo, Columbus & Cincinnati in 1892 gave the company a second, western route via Kenton into Columbus, completed 1893. The three lines drawn here are the T&OC's own names for them: the 197-mile Western Branch (Corning - New Lexington - Columbus - Marysville - Kenton - Findlay - Stanley Yard, Toledo), the 147-mile Eastern Branch (Thurston - Johnstown - Bucyrus - Fostoria - Stanley Yard), and the Southern Branch, the Kanawha & Michigan, running from Corning through Hobson, over the Ohio River on a 3,932-foot through-truss bridge at Point Pleasant and up the Kanawha Valley through Charleston. The New York Central leased the T&OC in 1928 and bought it outright in 1938. This fills in the last large blank area of the NYC system on the map: southeastern Ohio and the West Virginia coalfields.
sources: https://columbusrailroads.com/new/pdf/c&ccrr-part%202%20nyc.pdf ('Columbus and the Coal Country Railroads, Part II - The New York Central System', Columbus Railroads): the T&OC ran from southern West Virginia through Ohio's coal counties and Columbus to the Toledo Lakefront Coal Docks and carried almost a quarter of all coal moving on the NYC System; its main components were the 197-mile Western Branch from Corning through New Lexington, Columbus, Marysville, Kenton and Findlay to Stanley Yard in Toledo, the 147-mile Eastern Branch from Thurston (Milepost 160.8 on the Western Branch) through Johnstown, Bucyrus and Fostoria to Stanley Yard, and the Southern Branch from Corning through Hobson, over the Ohio River via a 3,932-foot through-truss bridge at Point Pleasant, WV, and up the Kanawha Valley through Charleston to Swiss; roundhouses and shops at Stanley Yard, Kenton, West Columbus, Bucyrus, Fultonham, Corning and Hobson in Ohio and at Charleston and Dickinson Yard in West Virginia; the NYC System peaked at 11,934 route miles in 1930

https://www.american-rails.com/toc.html (Atlantic & Lake Erie Railroad formed 1869 to connect Toledo with Pomeroy, Ohio, deliberately circumventing Columbus to the east to tap southeastern Ohio coal; reorganized as the Ohio Central in 1876 after building only 7 miles; receivership 1878; line completed Toledo to Middleport/Pomeroy 1882; rebranded Toledo & Ohio Central 1885; acquired the Toledo, Columbus & Cincinnati in 1892 giving a second route between Toledo and Columbus via Kenton, the Kenton-Columbus segment completed 1893; known as the 'Coal Line'; leased by the New York Central in 1928 and fully integrated in 1938)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toledo_and_Ohio_Central_Railway (T&OC operated 1885-1952; New York Central leasing from 1928 and purchase in 1938; predecessors listed as the Atlantic & Lake Erie, Atlantic & Northwestern, Ohio Central Railroad, Ohio Central Railway and Zanesville & Western)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Trains/ICC_valuations/Kanawha_and_Michigan_Railway (ICC valuation: main line Corning, Ohio to Gauley Bridge, W.Va.; Corning to Hobson 56.8 miles, Point Pleasant to Charleston 56.6 miles, Charleston to Malden 7.0 miles, Malden to Gauley Bridge 30.3 miles; 163.682 miles wholly owned; incorporated Apr 1890; as of Dec 31 1917 controlled through stock ownership by the Toledo and Ohio Central Railway, which was itself controlled by the New York Central Railroad)

https://www.american-rails.com/knwa.html (the Kanawha & Michigan was incorporated Apr 25 1890 and purchased the Charleston & Gauley Railway from Charleston to Dickinson on July 1 1890, extending to Gauley Bridge where it met the C&O and beginning operations Aug 21 1893; the Point Pleasant-Charleston line was completed in 1882, 56.6 miles, running through Putnam and Kanawha counties serving Buffalo, Red House, Poca, Raymond City and Dunbar; the corridor passed to Penn Central in 1968, Conrail in 1976 and Norfolk Southern in the 1999 Conrail split)
metadata.not_yet_sourced: Timetable frequencies for any era -- all headways here are estimates, and this was overwhelmingly a freight railroad, so the headways stand in for coal-train density rather than passenger service. Also not drawn or sourced here: the T&OC's many coal branches (the Buckingham Branch Glouster-Drakes-Shawnee, the 34-mile Hitop Branch out of Charleston, the Bailey Run and Sugar Creek & Athens, the Zanesville & Western and the Columbus, Shawnee & Hocking lines east of Columbus), and the exact abandonment dates of the segments that are gone today.
geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap (via Overpass API), ways tagged railway=rail/abandoned/disused/razed/dismantled, routed between the town waypoints named in the Columbus Railroads source with a shortest-path search over the OSM rail graph. Much of this network is still active freight track (Norfolk Southern and CSX), so most of it traces onto real rails; abandoned stretches depend on OSM's abandoned-railway coverage.
